title: Does the Internet Change How We Read and Think?
metaTitle: Does the Internet Change How We Read and Think?
metaDescription: Online reading favours skimming and scanning over deep reading. The evidence is suggestive, not settled — here is the honest picture.
keyFinding: The internet appears to encourage a skimming, scanning style of reading over slow, deep, linear reading, but the evidence that it has rewired our brains is suggestive rather than settled.
honestAnswer: The internet does seem to change how we read — nudging us toward skimming, scanning, and jumping between sources rather than reading slowly and linearly. Whether it has fundamentally rewired our capacity for deep thought is a much bigger claim, and there the evidence is suggestive but far from settled. The honest answer is that reading behaviour online clearly differs from deep reading on the page, while the deeper question of permanent cognitive change remains open.

Online text is built for movement — hyperlinks, headings, snippets, and an endless next thing — and our reading adapts to it. We get good at rapidly extracting gist and locating information. The open worry, articulated most prominently by Nicholas Carr and explored by reading researcher Maryanne Wolf, is that practising this fast, fragmented mode might make sustained, immersive 'deep reading' harder. That worry is plausible and partly supported, but it is not a proven, irreversible fact.
whatDataShows: Studies of online reading behaviour, including work by Ziming Liu, find that people read digital text differently: more skimming and scanning, more jumping around, spotting keywords, and reading non-linearly, with less sustained, in-depth reading than on paper. This is a reasonably consistent description of how screen reading happens, even if the long-term consequences are less clear.

Maryanne Wolf's work on the reading brain emphasises that deep reading — the slow, immersive, reflective engagement that supports inference, empathy, and critical analysis — is not innate but built through practice, and therefore could in principle be weakened if we practise it less. Nicholas Carr's 'The Shallows' (2010) popularised the argument that the web's design trains distraction and shallow processing. These are influential, carefully argued cases, but they are partly interpretive rather than the verdict of settled experiments.

Some experimental evidence complicates the simple 'screens are worse' story. Several studies and meta-analyses find that comprehension can be somewhat better on paper than on screen, especially under time pressure and for demanding texts — a difference sometimes called the screen inferiority effect — but the gaps are not always large or consistent, and depend heavily on the task, the reader, and how reading is measured. The fair summary is that medium and habit matter, but the research is mixed, evolving, and resistant to sweeping conclusions.
whyItFeelsDifferent: It feels like the internet has shortened our attention because the difficulty is so noticeable: sitting with a long, dense book can feel harder than it used to, and the pull toward checking, clicking, and switching is real. That felt experience is genuine, even where the underlying brain-change claim is uncertain.

The environment also constantly rewards the shallow mode. Online text is engineered to be scannable and to offer a more interesting next link, so the fast, fragmented style is reinforced thousands of times a day, while deep reading is rarely prompted by anything. We naturally drift toward the behaviour the environment keeps rewarding, and then experience that drift as a change in ourselves.

And we tend to attribute a diffuse sense of distraction to a single cause. 'The internet ruined my attention span' is a tidy story for a messy mix of habits, fragmented schedules, stress, and constant interruption. The web is a real part of the picture, but the feeling of changed reading is broader than any one clean mechanism the research has nailed down.
whatResearchSaysToDo: Because deep reading appears to be a practised skill, the most consistent implication is simply to practise it: setting aside uninterrupted time for sustained, linear reading of demanding material. Wolf's framing suggests the deep-reading capacity is maintained by use, so deliberately exercising it is the most direct response to worries about losing it.

Reducing interruptions during reading has clearer support than the broad rewiring claim. The well-established attention research shows that interruptions and task-switching degrade comprehension and focus, so reading in a setting without constant notifications and tabs is a reasonable, evidence-aligned step regardless of how the bigger debate resolves.

Matching the medium to the goal also fits the evidence: skimming and scanning are genuinely useful for locating information, while deep reading suits understanding and reflection. The point is not that screens are bad and paper is good, but that the fast mode and the slow mode are different tools, and it helps to choose deliberately rather than always defaulting to the scannable one.
whatDoesNotHelp: Treating the rewiring claim as proven fact does not help, because it overstates evidence that is genuinely mixed and can tip into fatalism — the belief that your attention is permanently broken, which the research does not support. Deep reading appears trainable, not destroyed.

Assuming screens are uniformly worse than paper is also not well supported. Comprehension differences exist but are inconsistent and task-dependent, and plenty of demanding reading happens perfectly well on screens. Swearing off digital reading entirely treats a nuanced, contested finding as a blanket rule it is not.

Conversely, dismissing the concern entirely — insisting nothing has changed — ignores the reasonably consistent finding that online reading behaviour really does skew toward skimming and switching. The honest position sits between the panic and the dismissal: behaviour has shifted, deep reading is worth protecting, and the strong brain-change claims remain unproven.
realNumbersInContext: This is a topic where precise numbers should be treated with real caution, because the strongest claims are interpretive rather than the product of clean, settled experiments. What is reasonably well supported is qualitative: online reading tends toward skimming, scanning, keyword-spotting, and non-linear movement, with less sustained deep reading than on paper, as documented in Ziming Liu's research.

On comprehension, meta-analytic work suggests a modest tendency for paper to outperform screens on demanding or time-pressured reading — the screen inferiority effect — but the gaps vary widely and are not always found. The fair takeaway is that the medium and your reading habits matter somewhat, that deep reading is a practised and protectable skill, and that anyone claiming the internet has definitively rewired the human brain is reaching well beyond what the evidence can currently bear.
keyTakeaways: Online reading behaviour clearly skews toward skimming, scanning, and non-linear jumping.
That behavioural shift is better established than the claim that the internet has rewired our brains.
Comprehension can be modestly better on paper for demanding texts — the screen inferiority effect — but the gaps are inconsistent.
Deep reading appears to be a practised, trainable skill, not something permanently lost.
The honest position sits between panic and dismissal: behaviour has shifted, deep reading is worth protecting.

faqs.question: Has the internet rewired our brains?
faqs.answer: That strong claim is suggestive but not proven. Writers like Nicholas Carr argue the web trains distraction and shallow processing, and Maryanne Wolf notes deep reading is a practised skill that could weaken with disuse. But this is partly interpretive, and the experimental evidence for permanent rewiring is mixed and far from settled.

faqs.question: Do we really read differently online?
faqs.answer: Behaviourally, yes — fairly consistently. Studies including Ziming Liu's find online reading skews toward skimming, scanning, keyword-spotting, and jumping around, with less sustained in-depth reading than on paper. That shift in behaviour is better established than any claim about permanent change to our underlying capacity.

faqs.question: Is reading on paper better than on screens?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, modestly. Meta-analyses suggest comprehension can be a bit better on paper, especially for demanding texts under time pressure — the screen inferiority effect — but the gaps are inconsistent and depend on the task and reader. It is not a blanket rule that screens are worse.

faqs.question: Can I get my deep-reading ability back?
faqs.answer: The research framing is encouraging here: deep reading appears to be a trainable, practised skill rather than something permanently lost. Setting aside uninterrupted time for sustained, linear reading of demanding material is the most direct way to exercise and maintain it.

faqs.question: What actually harms reading focus the most?
faqs.answer: The best-established culprit is interruption and task-switching, which clearly degrade comprehension and concentration. Reading without constant notifications, tabs, and pings has stronger evidence behind it than the broad brain-rewiring claim, and is worth doing regardless of how that larger debate resolves.
